125 percent.

That is Snowflake's net revenue retention as reported in their most recent filings. Datadog sits around 120. These are the numbers the software industry points at to prove that net retention is the most important metric in the business, and that a great NRR figure is the signature of a great customer success function.

Here is what almost nobody says out loud about those two numbers.

No quarterly business review produced them. No success plan produced them. No account manager ran a play that moved Snowflake from 118 to 125. Those figures are what happens when a customer pays for compute and storage they consume, and they consume more of it every quarter because their own business is generating more data. The pricing model is doing the retention. The meter is the motion.

Snowflake could dismiss its entire customer success organisation tomorrow and still post a healthy NRR next quarter, because the number is largely a function of customer workload, not customer relationship. That is not a criticism of their team. It is a description of how consumption economics work.

And if that is true at the top of the market, it is true in your business too.

## The Core Problem: You Cannot Tell What You Earned

Under a traditional subscription, expansion usually requires a human. Someone sells more seats. Someone negotiates a bigger tier. There is a motion, and you can trace it.

Under consumption pricing, the pricing model expands on its own. Usage goes up because the customer's business is growing, and the invoice follows. Your team may not have touched it at all.

So the critical question becomes: can you tell the difference between the retention you caused and the retention you happened to be standing next to when the meter ticked up?

Most teams cannot. They take credit for all of it. And that self-deception has a cost, because the same meter that hands you expansion you never earned can hand you contraction you never see coming.

## A Real Decomposition

Let me walk through the mechanics. The numbers here are changed, but the shape is drawn from real consumption-priced enterprise accounts.

An account renews on a consumption contract. Last year it burned one million dollars in usage. This year the dashboard shows it landing at 1.18 million. That is a 118 percent expansion. The account manager books it as a win. It goes in the review deck. It goes in the board prep as evidence the team is driving growth.

Now decompose it.

Of that 180,000 dollars in growth, 155,000 arrived in a single ten-week window in the spring. Pull the usage logs and the reason is obvious. The customer ran a data migration off a legacy platform, and every record they moved passed through the meter as data ingest. Nobody on the customer success side planned it, influenced it, or even knew it was happening until the invoice moved.

That is 155,000 dollars of pure metered retention. The pricing model earned it. The team did not.

The remaining 25,000 might be earned. Maybe someone drove real adoption of a new feature. Maybe a workflow the team designed pushed more volume through the platform. That part you can defend.

## Why This Should Worry You

Here is the uncomfortable flip side.

The meter reports churn last. The dollar number keeps telling a lovely story long after the underlying usage has started to decline. Because usage is billed in arrears, and because a single burst of activity can mask a slow bleed, the dashboard stays green while the account is quietly walking out the door.

That 118 percent account did not churn at renewal. It churned months earlier, in the usage graph, while everyone was still celebrating the expansion. The renewal was simply the day the team found out.

If you only watch dollars, you are watching the last indicator to move. By the time it turns red, your window to act has usually closed.

## The Framework: Metered vs. Earned Retention

The fix is a subtraction you can run this week. Here are five moves.

### 1. Decompose your biggest expansion account

Separate the usage growth a specific action caused from the growth that just happened. The migration that passed through the meter is not your win. Be honest about the split.

### 2. Label every healthy account as earned or metered

Earned means a documented action moved the account. Metered means the customer's own workload moved it. You will be surprised how much of your green is metered.

### 3. Switch your leading indicator to usage velocity

Stop treating dollars as your early warning system. Dollars report churn last. The rate of change in usage reports it first. Watch the velocity, not the invoice.

### 4. Build the two-line report before anyone asks

For your next board or finance conversation, show two numbers. Earned retention: the part your team caused. Metered NRR: the part the pricing model caused. Bringing this before someone else surfaces it is what separates a leader from a reporter.

### 5. Redeploy attention off metered accounts

Take one metered account off your best manager's heavy-touch list. It is riding the meter without them. Move that attention to an account you can actually influence, or to a declining account where there is still time to reverse the trend.

## The Point Is Not Smaller Numbers

This is not about shrinking your NRR or diminishing your team. It is about knowing which numbers you can defend when the meter turns against you.

A number you earned is a number you can protect. A number you happened to be standing next to will leave without warning, and it will take your credibility with it.

Go find out which of your healthy accounts are already declining underneath a green dashboard. Then go earn the retention you keep taking credit for.
